account: A small grey and white plover with a bill that bends to the right, the only bird in the world with a sideways-curved bill. It breeds on the braided gravel riverbeds of Canterbury and Otago in spring and summer, and feeds by sweeping the bill under stones for insect larvae. After breeding, most birds fly north to the harbours of the Firth of Thames and Kaipara, where flocks wheel in tight formation over the tidal flats.

A small plover of beaches and riverbeds. In the breeding season the adult has a narrow black band across the neck and a broad chestnut band across the breast. It breeds throughout New Zealand. After breeding, many birds from the South Island cross the Tasman Sea to winter in south-eastern Australia, which makes it a rare east-to-west migrant across that sea.

A large olive-green parrot of the Southern Alps, with orange-red under the wings. It is the only alpine parrot in the world. Kea are bold and curious: they investigate cars, packs and huts, and solve puzzles in captivity. The diet includes roots, berries, insects and carrion. Its loud call, a long 'kee-aa', gives the bird its name.

A forest parrot, olive-brown with crimson under the wings and on the belly. It moves noisily through the canopy in small groups, and feeds on fruit, nectar, seeds, sap and grubs dug from wood. Introduced predators reduced it to offshore islands and large forests, but fenced sanctuaries in Wellington and elsewhere have brought it back to cities.

A large, flightless, nocturnal parrot with moss-green feathers and an owl-like face. It is the heaviest parrot in the world. Males gather at display courts and make deep booming calls that carry for kilometres. It breeds only in years when rimu trees fruit heavily. All living birds are on predator-free islands and are managed one by one.

A large, flightless rail with deep blue and green plumage and a heavy red bill. It grazes on tussock bases and fern rhizomes in alpine grassland. It was thought extinct until its rediscovery in the Murchison Mountains of Fiordland in 1948. Today birds live in Fiordland, at sanctuaries and on predator-free islands.

A flightless, nocturnal bird with coarse brown feathers like hair, and nostrils at the tip of its long bill. It finds worms and insect larvae by smell. The female lays one of the largest eggs relative to body size of any bird, and the male incubates it. It lives in forest and scrub of the North Island.

A dark honeyeater that shines green and blue in sunlight, with two white tufts at the throat. It sings a complex song of bells, clicks, wheezes and notes too high for people to hear, and it can mimic other birds. It feeds on nectar of flax, kōwhai and pūriri, and defends flowering trees against other birds.

An olive-green honeyeater whose clear, bell-like song is a well-known sound of New Zealand forests. Captain Cook's crew described the dawn chorus of bellbirds as sounding like small bells. It feeds on nectar, fruit and insects, and lives in forest, scrub and gardens on both main islands.

A small, restless flycatcher that fans its long tail and follows walkers to catch the insects they disturb. Most birds are grey-brown with a buff belly, but a black form is common in the South Island. It lives in forest, scrub and gardens throughout New Zealand. The grey fantail of Australia, once treated as the same species, is now a separate species.

A large pigeon with an iridescent green and purple head and a clean white breast. Its wingbeats make a loud whooshing sound. It is the only bird left in New Zealand that can swallow the large fruits of trees such as taraire and tawa, so it is important for the spread of their seeds.

A small cuckoo with metallic green upperparts and a white breast with bronze bars. Its upslurred whistle is heard in New Zealand in spring. It lays its eggs in the nests of the grey warbler. Birds that breed in New Zealand spend the southern winter in the Solomon Islands and the Bismarck Archipelago, a sea crossing of about 3,000 km.

A large, slim cuckoo with a long barred tail, brown above and streaked below. It breeds only in New Zealand, where it lays its eggs in the nests of whitehead, yellowhead and brown creeper. In the southern winter it spreads across a vast area of the tropical Pacific, from Palau to French Polynesia.

A black and white wader with very long pink legs and a thin black bill. It feeds by picking insects and small crustaceans from shallow water and wet mud. It breeds in wetlands, riverbeds and pasture throughout New Zealand and Australia. It hybridises with the critically endangered black stilt in the Mackenzie Basin.

A stilt with entirely black plumage and long red legs, one of the rarest wading birds in the world. It breeds on the braided rivers and wetlands of the Mackenzie Basin. Predators, habitat loss and hybridisation with the pied stilt reduced the wild population to a few dozen birds. A captive breeding programme now releases young birds every year.

A black and white oystercatcher with a long orange-red bill. It breeds inland on South Island riverbeds and farmland in spring, then moves to northern harbours for the rest of the year. It uses its bill to open shellfish and to probe for worms. Its numbers increased greatly in the twentieth century.

One of the largest seabirds, with a wingspan of about three metres. Most breed on Campbell Island, and a small colony breeds on the mainland at Taiaroa Head on the Otago Peninsula. A pair raises one chick every two years. Between breeding attempts, birds circle the Southern Ocean and feed off the coasts of Chile and Argentina.

A penguin with pale yellow eyes and a yellow band that runs from the eyes around the back of the head. It nests in coastal forest and scrub, apart from its neighbours, on the south-east coast of the South Island, Stewart Island and the sub-Antarctic islands. Disease, warmer seas and fishing bycatch have caused a steep decline on the mainland.

A dark, slender shearwater with silvery underwings. It breeds in burrows on islands around southern New Zealand, where Rakiura Māori harvest the chicks as tītī. After breeding, birds make a figure-of-eight migration around the Pacific Ocean, to the waters off Japan, Alaska and California, and return in the southern spring.

A small, fast falcon that hunts birds in flight through forest and over open hill country. It is dark brown above with a streaked buff breast and rufous thighs. It nests on ledges, in trees and on the ground in pine plantations, which now hold a large part of the population. It defends its nest fiercely against people.

A small olive-green bird with a ring of white feathers around each eye. It colonised New Zealand from Australia in the 1850s without human help, and is now one of the most common birds there. In winter, flocks feed on fruit, nectar and the fat that people put out in gardens.

A swallow with glossy blue-black upperparts, a rust-red face and throat and a deeply forked tail. It is a common bird of open country in southern Australia. It arrived in New Zealand on its own in the 1950s and spread quickly. It builds a cup of mud under bridges and the eaves of buildings.

A large brown hawk that glides slowly low over open country and wetlands, with its wings held in a shallow V. It eats small mammals, birds, frogs, insects and carrion, and is often seen at roadkill. Old birds are pale, almost cream, below. It is common in New Zealand, Australia and many Pacific islands.

A large goose-like duck. The female has a white head and the male is almost black, which is unusual among ducks. Pairs stay together for life, and both call loudly when disturbed. It grazes on pasture and short grass and has become more common since farms replaced forest.

A blue-grey duck of fast, clear mountain rivers, with a pale pink bill and a chestnut-speckled breast. It feeds on insect larvae that it scrapes from rocks in the current. The male's whistle, 'whio', gives the bird its Māori name. Stoats take its eggs and nesting females, so it survives best where traps are set.

A large wader with a long, slightly upturned bill. Birds of the Alaskan population make the longest known non-stop flight of any land bird: from Alaska across the Pacific to New Zealand in about nine days. In spring they fly north to the Yellow Sea, refuel on its tidal flats, then continue to Alaska to breed.

A stocky, medium-sized sandpiper, grey in the non-breeding season and brick-red in breeding plumage. It breeds in the high Arctic and migrates in large flocks to coasts in the southern hemisphere. Each flyway depends on a few staging sites: the Yellow Sea for birds that winter in Australia and New Zealand, and Delaware Bay for birds that winter in South America.

A stocky, short-legged wader with a short wedge-shaped bill and harlequin black, white and chestnut plumage in summer. It turns over stones, seaweed and shells to find food. It breeds in the Arctic and winters on coasts on every continent except Antarctica.

A large, stocky kingfisher of eastern Australia, best known for its loud laughing call, which family groups give together at dawn and dusk. It does not need water to hunt: it watches from a perch and drops onto snakes, lizards, insects and small mammals. Young birds from earlier broods help their parents to raise new chicks.

A black and white bird of open country and towns across Australia and southern New Guinea, with a rich, flute-like carolling song. Groups defend territories all year. In spring a small number of males swoop at people who come near their nest. It feeds on the ground, mostly on insects and their larvae.

A tiny bird with a long, cocked tail. In the breeding season the male has a bright blue crown, cheeks and back. It lives in groups with a dominant pair and helpers. Although pairs are socially bonded, many chicks are fathered by males from other groups, and males show yellow petals to females outside their group.

A noisy, fast-flying parrot with a blue head, a red and yellow breast and a green back. Flocks feed on nectar and pollen with a brush-tipped tongue, and gather at night in large, loud roosts in city trees. It was once treated as part of the same species as the coconut lorikeet of Melanesia.

A lorikeet of the islands of Melanesia, from New Guinea to Vanuatu and New Caledonia. Its plumage is like that of the rainbow lorikeet but with a darker blue-black head. Until recent revisions the name Trichoglossus haematodus covered the rainbow lorikeet of Australia as well, so many older Australian records carry this name.

A large white cockatoo with a yellow crest that it raises when alarmed or excited. Flocks feed on seeds, roots and fruit, and post sentinels in trees that screech an alarm. In Sydney, birds have learned to open the lids of wheelie bins, and the skill has spread from suburb to suburb by social learning.

The tallest bird in Australia, flightless, with shaggy grey-brown feathers and long legs that can carry it at 50 km/h. It wanders widely across the inland in search of fruit, seeds and insects, and follows rain. The male incubates the eggs for about eight weeks without eating, then cares for the striped chicks for months.

A pink and grey cockatoo that is common across most of Australia. Flocks feed on grass seeds on the ground and in farm paddocks, and have spread with agriculture into cities. Pairs often stay together for life. Birds are known for acrobatics on power lines and in the rain.

A slim bee-eater with bright green, blue and gold plumage, a black eye-stripe and long central tail feathers. It catches bees, dragonflies and other flying insects in the air. It nests in tunnels that it digs in sandy banks. Birds from southern Australia migrate north to northern Australia, New Guinea and Indonesia for the winter.

The largest wader in the world, with a very long, down-curved bill that it uses to pull crabs and worms from deep burrows in mudflats. It breeds in north-eastern Asia and spends the non-breeding season on coasts of Australia. The loss of tidal flats in the Yellow Sea, where it stops on migration, has caused a steep decline.

A medium-sized sandpiper with a rufous cap and a chestnut tint to the breast. It breeds in north-eastern Siberia and is one of the most common migratory waders on freshwater and coastal wetlands of Australia from September to April. Unlike most waders it often feeds on inland wetlands and flooded grassland.

A sparrow-sized sandpiper, the smallest common wader in Australia. In breeding plumage the face and neck are rufous. It breeds in north-eastern Siberia and western Alaska and flies more than 10,000 km each way to the coasts of Australia, where large flocks feed on the mudflats with fast, short steps.

A stocky bowerbird. The adult male is glossy blue-black with violet eyes. He builds an avenue of sticks on the forest floor and decorates it with blue objects: feathers, flowers and, near people, bottle caps and pegs. He paints the inner walls with chewed plant matter. Females visit several bowers before they choose a mate.

A large, pheasant-like songbird of the moist forests of south-eastern Australia. The male has a long tail of lace-like feathers that he spreads over his head when he displays on a mound of earth. Both sexes are skilled mimics and copy the songs of many forest birds, and sometimes sounds made by people.

The largest bird of prey in Australia, dark brown to black, with a long wedge-shaped tail and a wingspan of more than two metres. It soars for hours on thermals over open country. It hunts rabbits, wallabies and birds, and eats carrion, often at roadkill. Pairs build large stick nests that they use for many years.

A very large black and white pelican with the longest bill of any bird. Flocks fish together by herding fish into shallow water. When rain fills the inland salt lakes, tens of thousands of pelicans fly hundreds of kilometres to breed on their islands, then leave as the water dries.

A large plover with a yellow facial wattle and a sharp yellow spur on each wing. It nests on the ground in open grass, including school ovals and the roofs of buildings, and attacks people and dogs that come near its nest. Its loud, rattling call is often heard at night.

A black and yellow honeyeater with a scaled pattern on the breast and bare pink skin around the eye. It follows the flowering of eucalypts across south-eastern Australia. So few birds are left that young males no longer hear enough adults to learn the correct song, and some sing the songs of other species.

A small grass parrot with a bright green back, a yellow belly with an orange patch and a blue band on the forehead. It breeds only at Melaleuca in south-west Tasmania and crosses Bass Strait each autumn to winter on the salt marshes of Victoria and South Australia. Only a few dozen birds remain in the wild.

A dark shearwater that breeds in huge colonies in burrows on islands of south-eastern Australia and Tasmania. Its chicks are harvested as muttonbirds in Tasmania. After breeding, birds fly to the North Pacific and the Bering Sea and return to their colonies within a few days of the same date each year.

A small grey flycatcher with a long tail that it fans while it hunts insects in flight. It has white eyebrows, a white throat and white edges to the tail. It lives in forests, woodlands and gardens across Australia. It was once treated as the same species as the New Zealand fantail, so many older Australian records carry the name Rhipidura fuliginosa.

A large, grey sandpiper with heavy dark spotting on the breast in breeding plumage. It breeds in the mountains of north-eastern Siberia and spends the non-breeding season mostly in northern Australia. Almost the whole population stops in the Yellow Sea on migration, so the loss of tidal flats at Saemangeum in Korea caused a sharp fall in numbers.

A small sandpiper with a bill that widens at the tip into a spoon. It breeds only on the coastal tundra of Chukotka in the Russian Far East and winters on mudflats in Bangladesh, Myanmar and southern China. Only a few hundred pairs remain. A conservation programme hatches eggs in captivity and releases the young birds at the breeding grounds.

A tall white crane with black wings and neck and a red patch of bare skin on the crown. Pairs perform dances of leaps, bows and calls, which have made the bird a symbol of long life and fidelity in East Asia. A resident population in eastern Hokkaido survives because farmers began to feed it in winter in the 1950s.

A white spoonbill with a black face and a black, spoon-shaped bill that it sweeps from side to side through shallow water to catch fish and shrimp. It breeds on rocky islets off the west coast of Korea and in north-eastern China, and winters in Taiwan, Hong Kong, Japan and Vietnam. Annual counts have risen from a few hundred birds to several thousand.

A small olive-green bird with a white ring around each eye. It lives in woodland, parks and gardens in Japan, Korea and eastern China, and feeds on nectar, fruit and insects. In late winter it feeds on the nectar of plum and camellia flowers. It was introduced to Hawaii in 1929 and is now common there.

A small duck of wooded rivers and lakes in East Asia. The male has orange 'sails' on the back, orange whiskers and a red bill. It nests in holes in trees, and the ducklings jump from the nest to the ground soon after they hatch. Feral populations live in Britain and other parts of Europe.

A small sparrow with a chestnut crown and a black spot on each white cheek. Males and females look alike. In much of East Asia it is the common sparrow of towns and villages. In Europe it lives on farmland and at the edge of woodland, and its numbers fell sharply in the late twentieth century.

A large white stork with black flight feathers, a heavy black bill and red skin around the eye. It breeds in the Amur and Ussuri river basins of the Russian Far East and north-eastern China, and winters in the Yangtze valley. It became extinct in the wild in Japan and Korea, and reintroduced birds now breed again at Toyooka in Japan.

A small falcon. The male is dark grey with rufous thighs and white underwings, and both sexes have red legs and a red ring around the eye. It breeds in eastern Asia and makes one of the longest migrations of any bird of prey: across India and then the Arabian Sea to southern Africa, where flocks roost in towns.

A swallow with glossy blue upperparts, a red throat and long tail streamers. It is the most widespread swallow in the world and breeds across the northern hemisphere, often in barns and sheds. European birds winter in Africa south of the Sahara, and birds ringed in Britain are regularly found in South Africa.

A grey, hawk-like cuckoo whose two-note call announces spring across Europe. The female lays single eggs in the nests of reed warblers, meadow pipits and other small birds, and each female line specialises in one host. Adults leave for central Africa in summer, and the young birds find their way there alone weeks later.

A small, round bird with an orange-red face and breast. In Britain it is tame and follows gardeners for worms, but on the continent it is a shy woodland bird. Both sexes sing and hold territories in winter. Many birds from northern and eastern Europe migrate to the Mediterranean in autumn.

A small, agile tit with a blue cap, wings and tail, a yellow breast and a white face with a dark eye-stripe. It hangs upside down to take insects from twigs. It nests in holes and nest boxes, and times its large brood so that the chicks hatch when caterpillars are most abundant on the oaks.

The largest tit in Europe, with a black head, white cheeks and a yellow breast with a black central stripe. Its song is a loud 'teacher, teacher'. It is one of the most studied birds in the world: long-term studies at Wytham Woods near Oxford have tracked its breeding since 1947.

A dark, sickle-winged bird that spends almost its whole life in the air. It feeds, drinks, sleeps and mates on the wing, and a young bird may not land for two or three years after it leaves the nest. It nests in holes in old buildings across Europe, arrives in May and leaves in August for Africa south of the equator.

A tall white stork with black flight feathers and a red bill and legs. It nests on roofs, church towers and electricity pylons, and pairs greet each other by clattering their bills. Migrants avoid long sea crossings and soar on thermals over the Strait of Gibraltar or the Bosphorus. Many Iberian birds now stay all winter and feed at rubbish tips.

A slender, grey and white tern with a black cap and a blood-red bill. It breeds around the Arctic and spends the northern winter in the Southern Ocean near Antarctica, so it sees more daylight than any other animal. Tracking has shown that some birds fly more than 90,000 km in a year.

A small auk with a large, striped red, yellow and blue-grey bill in the breeding season. It nests in burrows on grassy cliff tops in the North Atlantic, and carries rows of sand eels crosswise in its bill to its chick. It spends the winter far out at sea, and loses the bright plates of its bill.

A thrush of woods and gardens. The male is black with an orange-yellow bill and eye-ring, and the female is dark brown. Its rich, fluting song is heard at dawn and dusk from rooftops. It was introduced to New Zealand and Australia in the nineteenth century, and is now common there.

A graceful bird of prey with a deeply forked rufous tail and long, angled wings. It eats carrion, worms and small mammals. Persecution made it extinct in England and Scotland, but reintroduction since 1989 has made it common again over the Chiltern Hills and other areas.

A large, dark eagle with white shoulders, found only in the Iberian Peninsula. It hunts rabbits, so the rabbit diseases myxomatosis and haemorrhagic disease reduced its food. Electrocution on power lines and poison baits killed many birds. Protection of nests and the insulation of power lines have increased the population to several hundred pairs.

A tall pink-white flamingo with a pink bill tipped with black and bright red and black wings in flight. It filters small shrimp and algae from salt lagoons with its head held upside down. It breeds in large colonies in a few places, such as Fuente de Piedra in Spain and the Camargue in France.

A pinkish-brown bird with a long, thin curved bill, black and white barred wings and a crest that it raises like a fan. Its soft call, 'oop-oop-oop', gives the bird its name in many languages. It probes the ground for insect larvae. Birds from Europe winter in Africa south of the Sahara.

A colourful bee-eater with a chestnut crown and back, a yellow throat and a turquoise breast. It catches bees and wasps in flight and removes the sting by beating them against a perch. It nests in colonies, in tunnels in sandy banks, across southern Europe, and winters in Africa.

A black and white plover with green and purple gloss on the back and a long, thin crest. In spring the male performs a tumbling display flight over farmland and calls 'pee-wit'. Its numbers on farmland in Britain have fallen by more than half since the 1980s as farming practices changed.

A stocky bird with glossy, spotted black plumage that shines purple and green. It is a skilled mimic. In autumn and winter, roosts of hundreds of thousands of birds form swirling flocks called murmurations. Introductions have made it one of the most widespread birds in the world, including in North America, Australia and New Zealand.

A small, stocky sparrow that lives close to people. The male has a grey crown, chestnut nape and a black bib, and the female is plain brown. It has followed people around the world, but in many European cities its numbers have fallen sharply, for reasons that are not fully known.

A small, plain olive-green warbler with a pale eyebrow and pale legs. Its sweet, falling song is one of the commonest sounds of spring in northern European woodland. It weighs about 9 g, but birds from Siberia fly up to 12,000 km to winter in eastern and southern Africa.

A small flycatcher. The breeding male is black and white with a white wing patch, and the female is brown. It nests in holes in oak woodland and readily uses nest boxes. It winters in West Africa. Because it arrives back at a fixed date, warmer springs have caused it to miss the peak of caterpillars in some regions.

A slim black and white wader with very long pink legs. It breeds in wetlands, salt pans and rice fields in southern Europe, Africa and Asia. European birds winter in Africa. The name Himantopus himantopus once included the stilts of Australia, New Zealand and the Americas, which are now separate species.

A powerful falcon with a dark hood and moustache, blue-grey back and finely barred underparts. It hunts birds in flight with a steep dive, the stoop, in which it reaches more than 300 km/h. The pesticide DDT caused its decline in the twentieth century. It now nests on city buildings and bridges on most continents.

A large fish-eating bird of prey, white below and dark brown above, with a dark stripe through the eye. It dives feet first into water and carries fish head forward in its talons. It occurs on every continent except Antarctica, and northern birds migrate long distances to the tropics.

A brown sunbird-like bird with a very long tail, found only in the fynbos of south-western South Africa. It feeds on the nectar of proteas and pollinates them. In the breeding season the male flies over his territory with his tail jerking and his wings making a rattling sound.

A black and white penguin with a black band across the breast and a pink patch of bare skin above each eye. It breeds on islands and a few mainland beaches of South Africa and Namibia, including Boulders Beach near Cape Town. Overfishing of sardines and anchovies has reduced the population by more than 90 % in a century.

A colourful roller with a lilac throat and breast, turquoise belly and long outer tail streamers. It perches on bare branches and posts in open savanna and drops on insects and lizards. In the breeding season it rolls and dives in display flights.

A very large, black, turkey-like hornbill with a red face and throat. Groups walk through grassland and savanna in search of insects, reptiles, frogs and small mammals. Their deep booming calls carry for several kilometres at dawn. A pair raises only one chick every few years, with help from other members of the group.

A tall, long-legged bird of prey of African grassland, with a crest of long black feathers like quill pens behind the head. It walks up to 30 km a day and kills snakes, lizards and rodents with fast, accurate kicks. It appears on the coat of arms of South Africa and Sudan.

A large, grey-brown ibis with a long, down-curved bill and green and purple gloss on the wings. Its loud 'ha-ha-de-dah' call is a familiar sound at dawn in African towns. It probes lawns and wet ground for worms and insect larvae, and has spread into cities with garden irrigation.

A large eagle with a white head, breast and tail, chestnut belly and black wings. It sits on trees by lakes and rivers south of the Sahara and catches fish from the surface. Its loud, ringing call is a symbol of African wetlands. It is the national bird of Zambia, Zimbabwe, Namibia and South Sudan.

A grey crane with a crown of stiff golden feathers, white cheeks and a red throat pouch. It is the only crane that roosts in trees. Pairs dance, bow and boom in the wet season. It lives in wetlands and grassland of eastern and southern Africa, where the drainage of wetlands has caused its decline.

The largest living bird, flightless, with a long neck and powerful legs that can run at 70 km/h. The male is black with white wing and tail feathers. Several females lay their eggs in one nest, which the dominant female and the male incubate. It lives in open savanna and semi-desert of Africa.

A starling with glossy blue-green upperparts, a chestnut belly, a white band across the breast and pale eyes. It is common and bold in the dry savanna and tourist camps of East Africa. It breeds cooperatively: helpers bring food to the chicks of the dominant pair.

A sunbird of southern and eastern Africa. The breeding male is metallic green with long central tail feathers and yellow tufts at the sides of the breast, and the female is olive-brown. It feeds on nectar of aloes, proteas and red-hot pokers, and catches small insects.

The smallest and most numerous flamingo, deep pink, with a dark red bill. It filters blue-green algae from the surface of soda lakes. Flocks of more than a million birds gather at lakes of the East African Rift, such as Lake Nakuru and Lake Bogoria. Most birds breed at Lake Natron in Tanzania.

A large yellow weaver of south-western South Africa. The male has an orange face in the breeding season and weaves a hanging nest of grass with a downward entrance tube. A male builds several nests in a season and shows each one to females, which inspect it before they accept it.

A brown vulture of African savanna with a white rump and a bare dark neck. Flocks find carcasses by watching other vultures from great heights. Poisoned carcasses set out for predators, and poisoning by poachers who do not want circling vultures to reveal their kills, have caused a fall of more than 90 % in three generations.

A small cuckoo. The male is glossy green with white spots on the wing and a red eye, and its call 'dee-dee-dee-deederik' gives the bird its name. It lays its eggs in the nests of weavers and bishops. Southern African birds move north to central Africa in the dry season.

A large eagle with a white head and tail and a heavy yellow bill, the national bird of the United States. It catches fish and also steals them from ospreys. DDT reduced it to about 400 pairs in the lower 48 states in the 1960s. After DDT was banned, the population recovered, and it left the endangered species list in 2007.

A large thrush with a grey-brown back and a brick-red breast. It hunts earthworms on lawns by sight. It is one of the first birds to sing at dawn in spring in North America. Northern birds move south in winter, and flocks feed on berries.

A tiny hummingbird. The male has a ruby-red throat that looks black in poor light. It is the only hummingbird that breeds widely in eastern North America. Before autumn migration it nearly doubles its weight with fat, which lets many birds cross the Gulf of Mexico in one non-stop flight of about 800 km.

A crested songbird. The male is bright red with a black face, and the female is buff with red on the wings and tail. Both sexes sing a clear whistled song. It lives all year in woodland edges, thickets and gardens of eastern North America and is the state bird of seven states.

A tall grey crane with a red crown. In March, more than half a million birds gather on the Platte River in Nebraska, where they roost in shallow channels and feed on waste corn before they fly north to breed in Canada, Alaska and Siberia. It was formerly placed in the genus Grus.

A large godwit with a long, slightly upturned bill. In breeding plumage it is dark chestnut below. It breeds in Alaska and Canada and flies non-stop over the Atlantic Ocean to winter in southern South America, mainly on the island of Chiloé in Chile and in Tierra del Fuego. In spring it returns through the Great Plains.
A common, large hawk of North America with a brick-red tail. It perches on poles and trees by roads and hunts rodents. Its hoarse, screaming call is often used in films for any bird of prey.

A crested blue jay with black and white markings and a loud, varied voice. It also imitates the call of the red-shouldered hawk. It stores acorns in the ground in autumn and is thought to have helped oaks spread north after the last ice age.

A large white owl of the Arctic tundra. Males are almost pure white, and females have dark bars. It hunts in daylight in the Arctic summer, mainly lemmings. In years when lemmings are few, birds move far south in winter. It was formerly placed in its own genus, Nyctea.

One of the largest flying birds, with a wingspan of more than three metres. It is black with a white collar and white patches on the wings. The male has a fleshy comb. It soars along the Andes and the coasts of Chile and Argentina, seldom flaps its wings, and feeds on carrion.

A pink flamingo with greyish legs and pink knees. It lives on salt lakes and lagoons of temperate South America, from the high Andes to the coasts of Argentina, Chile and Uruguay. It feeds by filtering small invertebrates from mud. Its colonies move from year to year as water levels change.

A black and white penguin with two black bands across the breast. It breeds in burrows and under bushes in large colonies on the coasts of Argentina, Chile and the Falkland Islands, such as Punta Tombo. In winter it migrates north along the coasts of Brazil and Peru.

A small, fiery orange hummingbird. It breeds further north than any other hummingbird, up to southern Alaska. Its migration is one of the longest of any bird relative to body size: a round trip of about 6,000 km between Alaska and Mexico, following the flowering of plants along the mountains.

A slim hawk of the western prairies of North America. Almost the whole population migrates in large flocks through Central America to winter on the pampas of Argentina, where pesticide poisoning killed thousands of birds in the 1990s. In Argentina it follows ploughs and eats grasshoppers.

A blackbird of hayfields. The breeding male is black below and buff and white above, the reverse of most birds. It breeds in North America and winters in the grasslands of South America, a round trip of about 20,000 km. It finds its way partly by the earth's magnetic field.
